content.title: Function Notation, Domain, and Range
content.overview: This guide covers the fundamentals of linear functions, focusing on understanding function notation $f(x)$, determining the domain (the set of input values), and determining the range (the set of output values).
learning_objectives: Understand and apply function notation $f(x)$ for evaluation
Identify the domain of linear functions in various contexts
Identify the range of linear functions in various contexts
Distinguish between discrete and continuous domains

sections.title: Function Notation
sections.content:
Function notation uses the symbol $f(x)$ to represent a function. Here, $f$ is the name of the function, $x$ is the input value (independent variable), and $f(x)$ is the output value (dependent variable) corresponding to $x$. In linear functions, $f(x)$ is usually equivalent to the $y$-value in a Cartesian coordinate system. For example, if $f(x) = 2x + 3$, then $f(4)$ represents the value of the function when $x = 4$, calculated as $2(4) + 3 = 11$.

![Function Processing Flow](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/f9517249-a51f-4f38-b209-bf8ec007d2d3-1786502033997-845.webp)

sections.title: Domain
sections.content: The domain is the set of all possible input values ($x$-values) for a function. For an abstract linear function $f(x) = mx + b$, the domain is typically all real numbers. However, in practical SAT word problems, the domain is often restricted by real-world conditions. For example, if $x$ represents time or the number of items, $x$ cannot be negative ($x \geq 0$).

sections.title: Range
sections.content: The range is the set of all possible output values ($f(x)$ or $y$-values) for a function. It depends on the domain and the slope of the function. If the domain of a linear function is restricted, we determine the range by substituting the endpoint values of the domain into the function.

sections.title: Discrete vs. Continuous
sections.content: When dealing with domain and range, it is essential to distinguish between data types. Discrete data refers to cases where values can only take specific isolated values (such as the number of people, which must be integers); continuous data refers to cases where values can be any value within a certain interval (such as weight or time).

worked_examples.question: Given the function $g(x) = -3x + 10$. If the domain of this function is restricted to $1 \leq x \leq 4$, find the range of the function.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Substitute the minimum value of the domain $x = 1$ into the function: $g(1) = -3(1) + 10 = 7$. Step 2: Substitute the maximum value of the domain $x = 4$ into the function: $g(4) = -3(4) + 10 = -2$. Step 3: Since the slope is negative (-3), the function decreases as $x$ increases. Therefore, the range consists of all values between these two output values, which is $-2 \leq g(x) \leq 7$.

worked_examples.question: A bookstore sells books for \$15 each. The function $f(n) = 15n$ represents the total cost of purchasing $n$ books. Describe the domain of this function.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify that the independent variable $n$ represents the number of books. Step 2: Consider real-world constraints; the number of books cannot be negative and must be an integer (you cannot buy half a book). Step 3: Therefore, the domain is all non-negative integers $\{0, 1, 2, 3, ...\}$. This is an example of a discrete domain.

common_mistakes: Confusing $f(x) = a$ with $f(a) = x$: $f(x) = a$ means finding the input given the output, while $f(a)$ means finding the output given the input.
Ignoring practical context: Forgetting that $x$ or $y$ cannot be negative in word problems.
Incorrectly including endpoints: Confusing 'greater than' ($>$) with 'greater than or equal to' ($\geq$) in inequalities.
exam_tips: If you see a solid dot on a coordinate axis, it indicates the endpoint is included ($\leq$ or $\geq$); an open circle indicates it is not included ($<$ or $>$).
For a linear function, if the slope is not 0 and the domain is all real numbers, the range is also all real numbers.
When solving composite functions like $f(g(x))$, calculate the value inside the parentheses first.
content.recap: Function notation $f(x)$ is a tool to describe the relationship between input and output. The domain is the set of valid $x$ values, and the range is the corresponding set of $f(x)$ values. On the SAT, always judge whether these sets are continuous intervals or discrete values based on the problem context.

knowledge_claims.content: In function notation $f(x)$, $f$ is the function name, $x$ is the input value (independent variable), and $f(x)$ is the output value (dependent variable).
In a Cartesian coordinate system, the value of $f(x)$ corresponds to the $y$-coordinate of a point on the graph.
The domain is the set of all possible input values ($x$-values) for a function.
The range is the set of all possible output values ($f(x)$ or $y$-values) for a function.
For a linear function $f(x) = mx + b$ (where $m \neq 0$) without specific contextual restrictions, both the domain and range are all real numbers.
In word problems involving physical quantities (such as length, time, or mass), the domain is usually restricted to non-negative numbers ($x \geq 0$).
A discrete domain consists of isolated values (such as integers), while a continuous domain consists of one or more intervals.
To determine the range of a restricted linear function, substitute the endpoint values of the domain into the function expression to find the corresponding output values.
On a function graph, an open circle indicates that the point is not included in the domain or range, corresponding to $<$ or $>$ in an inequality.
A common mistake is assuming the domain of all functions is all real numbers, while ignoring real-world restrictions in the problem regarding item counts or time.
